Samples were taken either as separate sites generally consisting of 6-8 samples or, if conditions permitted, as stratigraphic profiles with each sample taken from a separate bed at regular 1-2 m intervals. Stratigraphic intervals were measured with a Jacob’s Staff and an attached Abney level. Mostly two specimens, 2.5 cm diameter and 2.25 cm height, were sliced from each core. Up to three specimens from each site, or one specimen from each third sample in case of stratigraphic profiles, have been subjected to progressive thermal demagnetization studies. The heatings were done in air in a furnace described by McElhinny et al. (1971). Because of the complexity of magne- tization, all pilot specimens were progressively demagnetized in 12-18 steps with decreasing temperature intervals up to 685°C. The intensity of suscep- tibility was measured after each heating step on a Digico bulk susceptibility unit. The remaining specimens were subjected to partial progressive demag- 258 netization in 8-12 steps over a selected temperature interval. Care was taken to keep the specimens in a very much reduced magnetic environment since the specimens tended to acquire Viscous Remanent Magnetization

components and failure to isolate separate components completely, further AFdemagnetization was not pursued for the bulk of the samples. All magnetic measurements were made on a SCT 2-axis super-conducting rock magnetometer which was interfaced to a Digico mini-computer for immediate data reduction. Directional analysis of all specimen components was made by means of orthogonal projection figures (Zijderveld, 1967, 1975). RESULTS A limiting factor for remanence measurement of carbonate rocks in particular was a strong development of viscous m~etization after heating above 400-450°C. Because of the individual behaviour of the specimens during thermal demagnetization, laborious demagnetization series had to be run coupled with careful analysis of the orthogonal projection figures. Within a site and even within a sample, individual magnetic components often showed widely different blocking temperature ranges. Throughout this study and especially in the lower intensity carbonate samples it was observed that the dem~etization paths often bypassed the origin of the projection figure during breakdown of what can be interpreted as the last remaining magnetic component. INTERPRETATION A major problem during thermal analysis of especially the carbonate specimens was excessive increase in susceptibility and in VRM (Fig. 1.6T, U, V,) at temperatures well above 400°C. This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of exchange coupling with the o

case of carbonate samples with a weak initial intensity which are subsequently further reduced during the demagnetization process, formation of such a secondary magnetic component may make it impossible to determine the primary magnetic component. Most red-bed samples showed an increase in susceptibility (Fig. 1.6R) after prolonged heating at temperatures above 500-6OO”C. A notable exception were red-bed samples from the Parachilna Formation and from the top member of the Billy Creek Formation (Fig. 1.6S, Table 1.4), which showed a significant decrease in susceptibility after heating above 400°C. This may be due to inversion of m~haemite to haematite (Turner and Ixer, 1977). The individual behaviour of the specimens during thermal demagnetiza- tion was variable (Fig. 1.5). It was often found that specimens taken from the same sample showed widely different blocking temperature regions for magnetic components of similar direction. This may partly be due to initial presence of an intimate mixture of authigenic magnetic minerals (Larson and Walker, 1975) further enhanced by a large variability in thermomagnetic properties of the transformed phase upon oxidation (Ryabushkin, 1976). Therefore, I prefer to treat the specimen directions as the fundamental unit for calculation of mean directions

The occasional presence of both normal and reversed polarities of the same magnetic component in the same specimen (Fig. 1.7A), points to a fairly long period of acquisition of the characteristic magnetic component spanning at least the period of one polarity reversal. Such a prolonged acquisition of magnetization may be due to the formation of authigenic oxyhydroxides and haematite during diagenesis, and later dehydration and oxidation due to changes in Eh-Ph conditions and/or tectonic and thermo- chemical effects. For instance, Dijksman (1977) observed in Miocene red clay beds from central Spain that the same magnetic direction resided in both magnetite and a haematite magnetic phase. The latter was acquired with a time lag of several 100.000 yrs due to the effect of changing Eh-Ph condition in the CRM formation process. Dual polarity observations were also made in Billy Creek equivalent beds on Kangaroo Island and in some sequences in the Amadeus Basin (Section III). Cambrian-Early Ordovician age is further supported by observations of regional changes in metamorphic grade of especially the late Proterozoic Tapley Hill beds in the Adelaide “Geosyn- cline” by McKirdy et al. (1975). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). From a detailed interpretation of the magnetic anomalies (Tucker, 1972), two stages of acquisition of secondary remanent magnetization were identified. Before folding, the beds acquired a remanent magnetic component close to the plane of sedimentary layering in a direc- tion 135” _+1 0. After folding another secondary magnetic component was imposed, again close to the bedding but in a general direction normal to the trace of outcrop. The agreement both in time of acquisition and in direction of McKirdy et al’s (1975) earlier mentioned secondary magnetic component with the characteristic component B is striking.

Even this relatively mild degree of meta- morphism has profoundly affected the magnetic minerals. Basalts forming in the oceans today and fresh Tertiary basalts in general have magnetite or titanomagnetite contents of 1% or so, induced magnetizations of - lop3 emu cmP3, and en's > 1 (often >> 1). Their NRM's tend to be about 10 times those of related mafic intrusive rocks. The meta: volcanic rocks in Table 1 have emu I k I emu ~m-~: they contain 10 to 1000 times less magnetite than their modern-day equivalents. On average, their en's are very low, indicating a coarse grain size. Greenschist-facies metamorphism has been responsible for destroying the finer-grained, high-stability fraction of the magnetic minerals in the volcanics. Group 1 directions tend to have north (or south) declinations and intermediate (40-65") inclinations. Group 2 directions tend to have shal- low inclinations with east to northeast (or west to southwest) declinations. Reversals of the paleofield are recorded in both groups. The proportion of normal and reversed samples is variable and not close to 50:50, suggesting infrequent reversals. A few formations show only group 1 or only group 2 NRM's, but most have examples of both, frequently superimposed in individual samples. Superimposed (or multicomponent) NRM's were separable in two cases: (I) if one component was completely demagnetized at high AF steps, so that the remanence vector reached a stable endpoint direction or (2) if one component was not demag- netized at all over some AF range, usually at low AF steps, so that the direction of the other compo- nent could be deduced by the Zijderveld diagram vector-subtraction technique (Zijderveld 1967). Otherwise, although the magnetization vector fol- lowed a "remagnetization circle" (Halls 1976) joining groups 1 and 2, neither component could be isolated from the data and used in defining the mean group directions. st Range Complex, an east-west-trending layered mafic-ultrarnafic extrusive sequence in the central Abitibi Greenstone Belt, can be divided into three groups. Group 1 units contain a high-coercivity, high-blocking temperature (greater than 520°C) magnetite-dominated remanence characteristic of the complex (D = 280°, 1 = 2", k = 5.5, (rg5 = 11.8", virtual geomagnetic pole = 13"E, 7"s; isolated by both AF and thermal methods), in good agreement with the few previous results bearing on the Late Archean apparent polar wander path for North America. Group 2 units contain a low-coercivity, low-blocking-temperature (less than 310°C) scattered remanence residing in pyrrhotite. Often, both remanences coexist in a single lithology at a given site. Group 3 units contain distributed coercivity and blocking-temperature remanences, again residing in magnetite, that are more scattered but statistically identical to the mean group 1 direction. The order of magnetic blocking appears to have been group 1 before group 3 before group 2. The geologic setting of the Ghost Range suggests that it has remained essentially stable since emplacement and therefore the group 1 direction appears to reliably represent a Late Archean paleomagnetic pole. The area is now flooded so that future work is not possible. The limited geological and statistical data base makes interpretation of the results necessarily tentative. The dikes yield an A component pole at 84W, 74% from magnetization residing in higher stability domains, which likely reflects emplacement either at -2150 or -1825 or - 1650 Ma ago, and a B component pole at 33W, 4"s residing in lower stability domains, which likely reflects metamorphism during the Hudsonian Orogeny at - 1725 Ma, or, less likely, during Grenvillian uplift at -975 Ma. The volcanics appear to yield a prefolding C component pole at 28"W, 49"s that dates ex

- 1725 Ma. This fits with the high blocking temperatures of up to 550°C for the component. Con- versely, the B antipole also lies near the Grenville Orogeny loop of the APW path at -975 Ma and could be an uplift component. This fits with the subgreenschist alteration at most of the dikes and Park's (1977) observation of similar Grenvillian uplift components in most rock units of the Labrador Trough. Volcanics The C and D components of the Archean volcanics are both thermally unblocked at -555 + 15°C. Although the C component is more prevalent than the D, both appear equally stable, and hence either may be older. Also, their high blocking temperatures suggest that both were set before or during the Kenoran Orogeny, which deformed and regionally metamorphosed the volcanics prior to -2450 Ma. The volcanics strike at 260 + 10" and dip at 62 + 8"s at all sampling sites, so that the fold test is equivocal. Microfold structures show that the volcanics plunge at 35 + 5W. Redbeds are known to generally possess high stability of remanent magnetization, owing to the presence of hematite, which has made them of great interest for paleomagnetic studies. Experimental method and results The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of each specimen was measured with a digital spinner magnetom- eter. At each site two specimens from different cores were subjected to demagnetization in alternating freIds in steps of 50 m lWOe (5 or I0 mT') up to 800 0e (80 mT), to test for stability. In general, small changes in remanence direction were observed after each step. Four specimens per site were demagnetized in detail by heating, which was found to be more effective in removing viscous components oriented roughly in the present local field direction. A stable end point was reached in about 70% of the specimens (Figs. 3,5,6,8). The rest of the specimens from each site were heated in three or four steps in a selected temperature interval (normally 540-670°C) on the basis of the more detailed results obtained for the four pilot specimens. Table 1 shows that this treatment resulted in substantial improve- ments in the site grouping statistics, the best grouping being shown and used in the calculation of the paleopole position. The pole positions for Circum-Superior orogen rocks, the Proterozoic outliers, and the Sutton Lake inlier suggest: (1) a time-stratigraphic correlation between the LC-4 Sakami, Dieter Lake, Sutton Lake, and the upper part of the Belcher Island sequences; and (2) a time-stratigraphic correlation between the lower part of the Belcher Islands sequence and the Richmond Gulf sequence, which must be substantially older than group 1. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: 11, and 111) have dealt with paleomagnetic and rock magnetic properties of the late Archean Wabigoon gabbro of the Wabigoon volcanic belt and the 2580 20 Ma Shelley Lake granite of the Quetico gneiss belt, both of the Archean Superior Province in north- western Ontario. The present paper describes similar studies carried out on the Burchell Lake granite of the Shebandowan- Wawa volcanic subprovince, which lies to the east of the Quetico Subprovince. A location map is given in 11. The natural remanent magnetizations (NRM's) of the Bur- chell Lake and Shelley Lake granites have much in common. Type 1 NRM, which was argued to be the primary 2580 Ma magnetization of the Shelley Lake body, is the characteristic Burchell Lake NRM. Type 2 NRM, a late Proterozoic re- magnetization component found in about a dozen Shelley Lake samples, is identified in a few Burchell Lake samples, but is rather poorly defined, perhaps because NRM intensities tend to be an order of magnitude lower (geometric mean 45 x emu/cm3 (0.045 A/m)) than in the Shelley Lake granite (mean 300 X emu/cm3 (0.3 A/m)). The Burchell Lake pluton has not been dated radiometric- ally. Granitic bodies a few miles distant have K/Ar biotite ages in the range 2550-2610 Ma (e.g., Giblin 1964, p. 21). Dike interiors are fine to medium grained with intergranular to subophitic textures that consist of subequal amounts (about 40% each) of weakly zoned saussuritized plagioclase (labra- dorite) and clinopyroxene (mostly augite with minor pigeon- ite). Pyroxenes are variably altered to chlorite and uralite and many are also rimmed by blue-green amphibole. Interstitial quartz is always present and composes up to 7% of the rock, but olivine is absent. Minor biotite and apatite also occur. Opaque phases (up to about 10%) include Ti magnetite, ilmenite, and trace sulphides. The Ti magnetite usually shows ilmenite ex- solution lamellae and may contain fine hematite rods, sug- gesting a low-level deuteric oxidation state of C3 (Haggerty 1976). The directions are statistically different at the 0.05 confidence level (statistics from Tarling 1983). One pos- sible explanation is that the northwest dikes have been rotated counterclockwise relative to the north dikes during deformation along the KSZ, as suggested by Bennett et al. (1967). How- ever, the declination difference (- 15") is less than the change in dike trend (25-40"), so some of the variation in dike trend must be primary. Other explanations for the paleomagnetic data are that the northwest-trending dikes are of a slightly different age, or that the remanence vector is biassed into the plane of the dike (Strangway 1961). This latter possibility needs to be checked by detailed rock magnetic studies but was not revealed in a statistical study of worldwide paleomagnetic data obtained from dikes (Evans 1968). Structural and paleomagnetic data from the Hearst dikes support the model of crustal tilting associated with KSZ thrusting proposed by Percival and Card (1983) and indicate that this deformation occurred at least in part subsequent to dike intrusion (i.e., after 2.6 Ga). Dikes on the eastern side of the KSZ comprise: (1) 2.6 Ga north-trending Matachewan quartz tholeiites, (2) 2.15 Ga northeast-trending Preissac tholeiites, and (3) 1.15 Ga east- northeast-trending Abitibi alkali olivine basalts (Fahrig 1972; Card et al. 1981; Gates and Hurley 1973; Hanes and York 1979). Although several paleomagnetic studies have been done on these dikes (e.g., Strangway 1961, 1964; Larochelle 1966; Irving and Naldrett 1977; Buchan and Schwarz 1981; Schutts and Dunlop 198 l), a clear picture of variation in primary direc- tion and polarity within any one swarm has yet to emerge. Comparatively little is known about the dikes west of the KSZ. Information is largely confined to reconnaissance petrog- raphy and petrochemistry (Siragusa 1977; Thurston et al. 1977; Card et al. 1981). K-Ar ages on NW-trending dikes range from 2.4 to 1.4 Ga (Wanless et al. 1966; W. F. Fahrig, personal communication, 1984). Four lithologic units are studied in this paper: (I) porphyritic syenite, a nepheline-poor rock with phenocrysts of potassium feldspar in a groundmass of biotite, clino- pyroxene, and blue-green alkali amphibole; (2) malignite, an equigranular nepheline-clinopyroxene - potassium feldspar rock with abundant apatite; (3) hornblende syenite; and (4) biotite pyroxenite. The individual units, including baked- contact rocks, have distinctive natural remanent magnetization (NRM) properties as a result of their rather different propor- tions of coarse- and fine-grained pyrrhotite, magnetite, and hematite. There are two characteristic components of NRM. The re- verse or R component is a south-southwest, shallow, upward magnetization carried mainly by pyrrhotite and coarse-grained magnetite. The normal or N component is a northward, inter- mediate, downward magnetization carried by fine-grained magnetite. The R component has the same direction as the NRM of the 2630 Ma Matachewan diabase (Irving and Naldrett 1977), whereas the N component resembles the primary NRM of the 2580 Ma Shelley Lake granite (Dunlop 1984~). Segments chosen to represent remanence components were selected on the basis of lowest MAD value and if their directions were not part of a progressive directional change when compared with those of adjacent and overlapping segments. Introduction This note describes first results from a palaeomag- netic research program designed to investigate the Lower Palaeozoic geomagnetic field and the relation of the major crustal blocks in Australia. Recent inter- pretation [ 1, 2] of the geological history of southeast Australia, in terms of plate tectonics, have stressed the complex tectonic history the region suffered dur- ing the Lower Palaeozoic. Therefore, to successfully describe an apparent polar wander path for Australia for this period, it would seem that results may be bet- ter obtained from localities situated in the older crustal regions. Indeed, almost all Lower Palaeozoic investiga- tions have been carried out with material sampled from the Northern Territory and South Australia, viz. Cambrian [3, 6] and Ordovician [7]. If agreement be- tween the palaeomagnetic records for the Lower Pa- laeozoic from separate crustal regions within Austra- fia can be demonstrated, then the relationship of Australia to the rest of Gondwanaland may be clarified. Geological note The Amadeus Basin has been described [8] as a 500 mile-long intracratonic depression with an area of approximately 60 000 sq. miles. It contains Proterozoic, Cambrian, Ordovician, Silurian?,Devon- ian to Carboniferous and minor Permian deposits. It is estimated that 30 000 ft. of sedimentary rocks have been preserved. For palaeomagnetic investiga- tion, rock samples were collected from the Late Precambrian and Palaeozoic sequence which is expo- sed in Ellery Creek located at 133°E 23.8°S. The Creek has cut a north-south valley through the steeply south-dipping beds of the Palaeozoic sequence along the northern edge of the Basin. Results from the Arumbera Sandstone and the Hugh River Shale are described in this paper. Both rock units dip uni- formly southwards at about 70 ° . Exposed stratigraphic levels of the upper 600 ft. or so of the Arumbera Sandstone yielded samples. It consists of red-brown feldspathic sandstone with a medium- to fine-gained texture. ions of the deposits of the Coronation Geos yncline and associated aulacogen. These deposits record the phases of a classical geosynclinal cycle for which Hoffman has provided a beautiful interpretation in terms of an ocean-con- tinent plate interaction (Hoffman 1973). The Coro- nation loop appears, in part at least, to be the paleomagnetic signature of this cycle. The rate of motion relative to the pole, that is the rate of change of latitude, is about 5 cm year-'. The major defor- mation phase occurs during and after the deposi- tion of the Great Slave Supergroup, but before the deposition of the Et-Then Group, so the bend or hairpin of the Coronation loop corresponds to that deformational phase. During this deformational phase, the Coronation Geosyncline was in latitudes of about 25" (Seton Formation), moved to equa- torial latitudes (Christie Bay Group) and then back to a latitude of about 25" (Et-Then Group). Thus the major deformation phase of the Coronation Geo- syncline corresponds to a large change in direction of the motions of the Laurentian plate as recorded paleomagnetically between the Pearson and the Et-Then. The orogenic phase of the Coronation Geosyn- cline, which is dated about - 1800 Ma, appears to post-date certain Hudsonian events in th

useful physically recognizable boundary between the Aphebian and Helikian. The type loca- tion is the East Arm of the Great Slave Lake, and the pole change corresponding to the observed magnetic change is as described in Fig. 10. The current best estimate of the time at which this change occurred is - 1800 Ma. The Et-Then Group contains thin basic volcanic members (Hoffman 1968), acd hence, like the Pearson Formation, could possibly be dated, so that in principle the boundary could be more accurately fixed in time. NALDRETT Earth Physics Branch, Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, Ottawa and Department of Geology, University of Toronto, Toronto ABSTRACT Paleomagnetic results are described from three Archean rock units, and two sets of diabase dikes that intrude them. The magnetization of the country rocks is reset by intrusion of the diabase up to distances of about 80 m from contacts. The temperature reached during intrusion at this distance determined from thermal demagnetization is about 400°C, which is also the approximate temperature predicted from Jaeger's cooling curves assuming intrusion into cool rock. At greater distances other and presumably older magnetizations are found with a westerly direction. The oldest dykes (the Matachewan) have an age of - 2.6 Ga so that this westerly directed magnetization was acquired during the Archean. Its age, other than the fact that it is Archean, is not known, but by comparison with results from the Stillwater Complex it is estimated to be about - 2.8 Ga. The results are used along with previously published data to define in tentative fashion an apparent polar wanderin

ving each unit weight to obtain the mean for each sampling site. The overall averages for each rock unit are calculated giving unit weight to the mean of each sampling site. ABITIBI DIKES In their unaltered state these dikes consist of 50-60 modal percent plagioclase, 30% augite, 5-10% quartz and 5-7% opaques. The plagioclase is fresh and occurs as stubby to acicular laths up to 2 mm long, bearing an ophitic to sub- ophitic relationship to the enclosing augite, which is mostly replaced by chlorite, brown and green amphibole, and biotite. Quartz occurs interstitially to the plagioclase and pyroxene. Magnetite was the original opaque mineral occurring as equant grains up to 1 mm in diameter with ilmenite exsolved around the margins and parallel to [111]. In most samples this primary magnetite has been totally al- tered, leaving only the ilmenite lamellae with a matrix of very fine-grained poorly reflecting material that could not be iden- tified in polished section. Small amounts (0.5%) of pyrite are present, commonly associated with biotite. Trace quantities of pyrrhotite and chalcopyrite are also observed. NALDRETT Earth Physics Branch, Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, Ottawa and Department of Geology, University of Toronto, Toronto ABSTRACT Paleomagnetic results are described from three Archean rock units, and two sets of diabase dikes that intrude them. The magnetization of the country rocks is reset by intrusion of the diabase up to distances of about 80 m from contacts. The temperature reached during intrusion at this distance determined from thermal demagnetization is about 400°C, which is also the approximate temperature predicted from Jaeger's cooling curves assuming intrusion into cool rock. At greater distances other and presumably older magnetizations are found with a westerly direction. The oldest dykes (the Matachewan) have an age of - 2.6 Ga so that this westerly directed magnetization was acquired during the Archean. Its age, other than the fact that it is Archean, is not known, but by comparison with results from the Stillwater Complex it is estimated to be about - 2.8 Ga. Its age, other than the fact that it is Archean, is not known, but by comparison with results from the Stillwater Complex it is estimated to be about - 2.8 Ga. The results are used along with previously published data to define in tentative fashion an apparent polar wandering curve for the late Archean and early Aphebian which is referred to as Track 6. This polar path is of potential importance for stratigraphic correlations and for the tectonic history of late Archean time. For instance, it would provide information relating to the nature of the Kenoran Orogeny. Sampling was carried out during the summers of 1970, 1971, and 1973. It ought to be possible to retrieve original magnetizations in the Abitibi Greenstone Belt provided that magnetizations with high discrete blocking temperatures (that is square-shouldered thermal decay curves) can be located. The key observations required are the thermal decay characteristics. The metamorphism associated with the Kenoran Orogeny, is however not the only possible cause of remagnetization. Long- term mild reheating may have accom- panied either the intrusion of Proterozoic dikes, or burial beneath Huronian sedi- ments which may once have blanketed this area. Thus studies of dike contacts have been made, and one of the by- products of this work has been that we have been able to show, for the first time, that the characteristic magnetization di- rections of the Abitibi and Matachewan dike swarms were acquired at the time they were intruded. INTRODUCTION The purpose of this paper is to describe new paleomagnetic results from the Abitibi Greenstone Belt, and then to use them to construct a path of apparent polar wander (APW) for late Archean and early Aphe- bian time (approximately -2.3 to -2.8 Ga, Ga = 109y). This polar path is of potential importance for stratigraphic correlations and for the tectonic history of late Archean

study of palaeo- magnetism of Archean rocks of Laurentia was made by Berg (1970) on the Stillwater Igneous Complex. Estimates of the age of emplacement of the complex have been obtained by Nunes and Tilton (1971) who obtained -2.75 Ga by the U-Pb method from zircons in the basal zone, and by Mueller and Wooden (1976) who obtained -2.75 + 0.05 Ga for an Rb-Sr isochron from the contact aureole. (Rb-Sr ages in this paper are quoted for SRb decay constant of 1.39 x 10-11y-1.) Berg ob- tained some consistent magnetization directions, but the layering at his sites is approximately uniform so that it is not possible to use Graham's fold test (Graham 1949) to determine whether the magnetiza- tion was acquired before or after deforma- tion. Berg believed that the magnetization was acquired before deformation. It is equally possible that the magnetization was acquired after deformation. For example the thick Archean sills of the Chibougamau Greenstone Belt have mag- netizations which structural evidence shows were acquired after deformation (Ueno and Irving 1976). Ueno and Irving therefore considered these magnetizations to be somewhat younger than the Kenoran Orogeny, which in this area is determined by Rb-Sr isochrons to be about -2.6 Ga (Jones et al. 1974). PALEOMAGNETISM IN ABITIBI GREENSTONE BELT, AND ABITIBI AND MATACHEWAN DIABASE DIKES: EVIDENCE OF THE ARCHEAN GEOMAGNETIC FIELD1,2 E. IRVING AND A. J. NALDRETT Earth Physics Branch, Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, Ottawa and Department of Geology, University of Toronto, Toronto ABSTRACT Paleomagnetic results are described from three Archean rock units, and two sets of diabase dikes that intrude them. The magnetization of the country rocks is reset by intrusion of the diabase up to distances of about 80 m from contacts. The temperature reached during intrusion at this distance determined from thermal demagnetization is about 400°C, which is also the approximate temperature predicted from Jaeger's cooling curves assuming intrusion into cool rock. At greater distances other and presumably older magnetizations are found with a westerly direction. The oldest dykes (the Matachewan) have an age of - 2.6 Ga so that this westerly directed magnetization was acquired during the Archean. Its age, other than the fact that it is Archean, is not known, but by comparison with results from the Stillwater Complex it is estimated to be about - 2.8 Ga. The results are used along with previously published data to define in tentative fashion an apparent polar wandering curve for the late Archean and early Aphebian which is referred to as Track 6. Track 6 has a simple form, and there is no indication that the horizontal mobility of the crust in the late Archean was any greater than during the Proterozoic. This polar path is of potential importance for stratigraphic correlations and for the tectonic history of late Archean time. study of palaeo- magnetism of Archean rocks of Laurentia was made by Berg (1970) on the Stillwater Igneous Complex. Estimates of the age of emplacement of the complex have been obtained by Nunes and Tilton (1971) who obtained -2.75 Ga by the U-Pb method from zircons in the basal zone, and by Mueller and Wooden (1976) who obtained -2.75 + 0.05 Ga for an Rb-Sr isochron from the contact aureole. METHODS Samples were cored by gasoline drill and oriented by magnetic and solar compass. About five cores were drilled at each collecting site, and two cylindrical speci- mens were cut from each core. The remanent magnetization of the specimens was measured by spinner magnetometers. All specimens were demagnetized by step-wise heating, or by alternating fields (a.f. peak field strength are quoted) using the apparatus described by Roy et al. (1969, 1971, 1973). Demagnetization was carried in fields of less than two gammas. In some samples, particularly from the Dundonald sill, no coherent magnetization could be found; if the directions in specimens from the same sample disagreed by more than 40°, the results were rejected. Eight percent of samples collected were rejected on this basis. Results from each specimen are averaged to give means for each core. The core means are averaged giving each unit weight to obtain the mean for each sampling site. The overall averages for each rock unit are calculated giving unit weight to the mean of each sampling site. ABITIBI DIKES In their unaltered state these

study of palaeo- magnetism of Archean rocks of Laurentia was made by Berg (1970) on the Stillwater Igneous Complex. Estimates of the age of emplacement of the complex have been obtained by Nunes and Tilton (1971) who obtained -2.75 Ga by the U-Pb method from zircons in the basal zone, and by Mueller and Wooden (1976) who obtained -2.75 + 0.05 Ga for an Rb-Sr isochron from the contact aureole. (Rb-Sr ages in this paper are quoted for SRb decay constant of 1.39 x 10-11y-1.) Berg ob- tained some consistent magnetization directions, but the layering at his sites is approximately uniform so that it is not possible to use Graham's fold test (Graham 1949) to determine whether the magnetiza- tion was acquired before or after deforma- tion. For example the thick Archean sills of the Chibougamau Greenstone Belt have mag- netizations which structural evidence shows were acquired after deformation (Ueno and Irving 1976). Ueno and Irving therefore considered these magnetizations to be somewhat younger than the Kenoran Orogeny, which in this area is determined by Rb-Sr isochrons to be about -2.6 Ga (Jones et al. 1974). NALDRETT Earth Physics Branch, Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, Ottawa and Department of Geology, University of Toronto, Toronto ABSTRACT Paleomagnetic results are described from three Archean rock units, and two sets of diabase dikes that intrude them. The magnetization of the country rocks is reset by intrusion of the diabase up to distances of about 80 m from contacts. The temperature reached during intrusion at this distance determined from thermal demagnetization is about 400°C, which is also the approximate temperature predicted from Jaeger's cooling curves assuming intrusion into cool rock. At greater distances other and presumably older magnetizations are found with a westerly direction. The oldest dykes (the Matachewan) have an age of - 2.6 Ga so that this westerly directed magnetization was acquired during the Archean. Its age, other than the fact that it is Archean, is not known, but by comparison with results from the Stillwater Complex it is estimated to be about - 2.8 Ga. The results are used along with previously published data to define in tentative fashion an apparent polar wanderin

westerly directed magnetization was acquired during the Archean. Its age, other than the fact that it is Archean, is not known, but by comparison with results from the Stillwater Complex it is estimated to be about - 2.8 Ga. The results are used along with previously published data to define in tentative fashion an apparent polar wandering curve for the late Archean and early Aphebian which is referred to as Track 6. Track 6 has a simple form, and there is no indication that the horizontal mobility of the crust in the late Archean was any greater than during the Proterozoic. INTRODUCTION The purpose of this paper is to describe new paleomagnetic results from the Abitibi Greenstone Belt, and then to use them to construct a path of apparent polar wander (APW) for late Archean and early Aphe- bian time (approximately -2.3 to -2.8 Ga, Ga = 109y). This polar path is of potential importance for stratigraphic correlations and for the tectonic history of late Archean time. For instance, it would provide information relating to the nature of the Kenoran Orogeny. Sampling was carried out during the summers of 1970, 1971, and 1973. The Abitibi greenstone belt is relatively weakly metamorphosed, the grade of metamorphism varying from lower green- schist to prehnite-pumpellyite facies (

d survive the prehnite-pumpellyite and low greenschist facies metamorphism provided there has been no chemical change of the iron minerals. It ought to be possible to retrieve original magnetizations in the Abitibi Greenstone Belt provided that magnetizations with high discrete blocking temperatures (that is square-shouldered thermal decay curves) can be located. The key observations required are the thermal decay characteristics. The metamorphism associated with the Kenoran Orogeny, is however not the only possible cause of remagnetization. Long- term mild reheating may have accom- panied either the intrusion of Proterozoic dikes, or burial beneath Huronian sedi- ments which may once have blanketed this area. Thus studies of dike contacts have been made, and one of the by- products of this work has been that we have been able to show, for the first time, that the characteristic magnetization di- rections of the Abitibi and Matachewan dike swarms were acquired at the time they were intruded. The first important study of palaeo- magnetism of Archean rocks of Laurentia was made by Berg (1970) on the Stillwater Igneous Complex. OF KAMINAK DIKES 205 1 have no expression on aeromagnetic maps. The characteristic plagioclase phenocrysts range in size from a few millimetres to 5 cm or more. Generally they constitute a very few percent of the diabase, but locally they are crowded into zones parallel to the dike walls. Within the central part of the Kaminak Sub- province, the diabase dikes range from entirely fresh to partly or wholly altered. The fresh diabase dikes have dark, charcoal gray, chilled margins with microphenocrysts of clear plagio- clase and augite, and dark gray, medium grained cores with ophitic texture and glassy plagioclase phenocrysts. In thin section, clear plagioclase laths are seen to be partly enclosed by both augite and pigeonite. Early crystallized olivine is usually present in small amounts. Thin rims of brown hornblende border pyroxene grains locally. Quartz is absent. Opaque oxide grains are chiefly Ti-magnetite-ilmenite inter- growth; skeletal ilmenite grains are uncommon. In contrast, the more completely altered diabase dikes have greenish gray chilled margins and darker greenish gray, medium grained cores with clouded, dull white or yellow plagioclase phenocrysts. Thin sections reveal a variety of alteration products, although the original ophitic texture is usua

ellyite have been identified. In the central part of the Kaminak Sub- province, the distribution of fresh and altered dikes is apparently haphazard. Both fresh and altered dikes may occur in the same outcrop area, and fresh dikes may become altered along strike. To the north and south all the dikes become altered, and can be traced through zones of increasingly higher-grade metamorphic assemblages and structural degradation to where they are reduced to large boudins of amphibo- lite within migmatitic gneisses. The heavy dashed line in Fig. 1 delimits the first obvious metamor- phic effect; primary pyroxene has not been found in thin sections of diabase north of this line, nor has the metamorphic mineral stilpno- melane been found south of it. Sampling for the current paleomagnetic study was restricted to the area in Fig. 1 south of this line. Although many of the diabase dikes south of this line are altered, it seems likely that some, if not most, of this alteration was the result of deuteric hydration during original cooling, rather than being solely an effect of Hudsonian metamor- phism. The occurrence of secondary hydrous minerals in the altered diabases that would form only at higher metamorphic grade than the first appearance of stilpnomelane is evidence in th

may be due to greater susceptibility for argon loss from previously altered dikes than from fresh ones, or it may be due to variation in the amount of low grade recrystallization during the Hudsonian. Lamprophyre Dikes Gray lamprophyres with biotite phenocrysts occur as narrow dikes, generally less than 2 m wide, throughout the region from Hudson Bay to Lake Athabaska. In the Kaminak Sub- province, the lamprophyre dikes trend between north 70" east and south 60" east. They are commonly sinuous in detail, or form very narrow swarms of discontinuous dikelets. In several places they are full of rounded country rock xenoliths. In thin sections, the lamprophyre is seen to be composed primarily of K-feldspar and biotite with lesser amounts of quartz, albite, and pale amphibole, and accessory sphene, apatite, and calcite. The larger biotite pheno- crysts have colorless (phlogopitic?) cores and orange-brown frayed rims, and are commonly bent. Lamprophyre dikes cut all rock units within the area, with the exception of the northwest- trending Mackenzie diabase dikes. Unmeta- morphosed lamprophyre dikes cut cleanly across metamorphosed Kaminak dikes, now amphibolites with granular plagioclase augen in place of primary phenocrysts, in the vicinity of O'Neil Lake (Fig. 1).

The fresh diabase dikes have dark, charcoal gray, chilled margins with microphenocrysts of clear plagio- clase and augite, and dark gray, medium grained cores with ophitic texture and glassy plagioclase phenocrysts. In thin section, clear plagioclase laths are seen to be partly enclosed by both augite and pigeonite. Early crystallized olivine is usually present in small amounts. Thin rims of brown hornblende border pyroxene grains locally. Quartz is absent. Opaque oxide grains are chiefly Ti-magnetite-ilmenite inter- growth; skeletal ilmenite grains are uncommon. In contrast, the more completely altered diabase dikes have greenish gray chilled margins and darker greenish gray, medium grained cores with clouded, dull white or yellow plagioclase phenocrysts. Thin sections reveal a variety of alteration products, although the original ophitic texture is usually preserved. Groundmass pla- gioclase is commonly sericitized and associated with secondary epidote. The original pyroxenes are changed to uralitic amphibole with colorless cores and brownish outer-zones: discontinuous rims of blue-green hornblende are present locally. Clo

Secondary brownish biotite is commonly associ- ated with altered opaque oxide grains. In the central part of the Kaminak Sub- province, the distribution of fresh and altered dikes is apparently haphazard. PRELIMINARY RESULTS OF A STUDY OF THE PALEOMAGNETISM OF THE SUDBURY IRRUPTIVE INTRODUCTION The Sudbury Irruptive has inspired a voluminous body of geological literature and yet its mode of orig in still remains enigmatic from many points of view. F i gure 1, a simplified geo l ogical map, shows that the irrup­ tive has a roughly oval shape composed of an inner member of micropegma­ tite and an outer layer of a bas i c rock commonly referred to as norite. The rocks of both members are known to dip concordantly toward the centre of the structure and they are presently believed to be about 1700 m. y. old (Fairbairn et al., 1968). Previous studies on the paleomagnetism of the irruptive by Hood (1961) and Sopher (1963) pointed out that the mean directions of magnetiza­ tion in the south and north sections of the oval diverge appreciably from one another. This observation suggested to both authors that the present shape of the irruptive is partly due to post - irruptive tectonic activity. Sopher had also noted that the paleomagnetic directions obtained from the norite are considerably more consistent than those obtained from the micropegmatite but he did not make a quantitative appraisal of this observation. Finally, he noted that within sect

tive indicate that the mean directions of magnetization in th e North and South Ranges diverge significantly by about 40 degrees, in conformity with the pre­ vious observations of Hood (1961) and Sopher (1963). A large proportion of th e paleomagnetic data previously reported by Sopher satisfy the norms imposed on the data reported in the present study and can legitimately be combined with them. None of the previous paleo­ magnetic interpretations can yet be disputed or corroborated in the light of the above analysis but their basis and the planning of future work to test them is undoubtedly established more firmly. TRM could be acquired during initial cooling of an igneous body, and there are numerous examples given in the literature. A primary CRM is much less discussed, although studies by a few workers (e.g. Buddington and Lindsley 1964; Ade-Hall et al. 1965; Carmichael and Nicholls 1967; GrommC et al. 1969) indicate that this type of magnetization might be of frequent occurrence. For example, Buddington and Lindsley have shown that, in many rocks, some phases in the FeO-Fe20,-TiO, system do not reach equilibrium until cooling to tempera- tures as low as 650-550 "C. Since this is the range of blocking temperatures for hemoilmenite and titanomagnetite, the primary magnetization could easily be a CRM. Deuteric alteration at low temperatures could also produce CRM. Evidence for primary CRM might be found at some of the sites where the blocking temperatures of the primary magnetization C are clearly above the Curie point of magnetite, and range from 600 up to 675 "C in some instances. Indeed, in a recent review, Baag and Helsley (1974, p. 3308) concluded that "most paleomagnetic literature concerning red beds supports the view that the stable primary NRM of red beds was acquired at and/or soon after deposition". Furthermore, these authors point out that the presence of a gradual trend of intermediate directions between opposed polarity zones favours syndepositional acquisition of remanence. Despite these favour- able points, it is, of course, possible to devise later remagnetization schemes (e.g., movement of an isotherm or chemical front) that could give rise to the observed facts, and the problem cannot be completely resolved by reference to the Stark Formation data alone. The possibly primary nature of the remanence was discussed further in a companion paper (Evans and Bingham 1975), where results from strati- graphically adjacent formations were described. A paleomagnetic survey (34 sites, 200 core samples) of an Archean greenstone belt just north of the Grenville Front is described. Sixty per cent of the samples have blocking tem- peratures less than 400°C and remanent coercive forces predominantly below 100 Oe, and they provide no information about the Precambrian geomagnetic field. The other samples contain many magnetizations of which two (CS and CH) can be clearly recognized. The CS magnetization occurs in basic sills, and has high blocking temperature (550 to 650°C) and remanent coercive force (often exceeding 1000 Oe) and a direction (186°,--38 °) that is not significantly different from that in Matachewan diabase dikes (2690 m.y.). CS is thought to have been caused by uplift following the Kenoran orogeny and its age is prob- ably about 2600 m.y. No older magnetization has been found. The CH magnetization occurs in several different bodies and has a direction (119 °, +51 °) similar to that observed in rocks from other places close to the Grenville Front. CH has more variable blocking temperatures (200 to 650°C) and remanent coercive forces (200 to > 1000 Oe) and is con- sidered to have been acquired by heating during uplift of the highly metamorphose Gren- ville Province to the south. Uplift occurred about I000 m.y. ago, and the CH magnetiza- tion is considered to be of this age. Evidence is presented to support the suggestion that there was an extensive magnetization episode both within and adjacent to the Grenville Province at that time. Sixty per cent of the samples have blocking tem- peratures less than 400°C and remanent coercive forces predominantly below 100 Oe, and they provide no information about the Precambrian geomagnetic field. The other samples contain many magnetizations of which two (CS and CH) can be clearly recognized. This is associated with ilmenite as a separate phase and the mineralogy of the rock demonstrates that it has a low temperature metasomatic origin. This is associated with ilmenite as a separate phase and the mineralogy of the rock demonstrates that it has a low temperature metasomatic origin. [Traduit par le journal] Introduction The town of Gowganda is about 190 km north of Sudbury, Ontario (Fig. 1). From 1908 to 1972, native silver was mined near the town from narrow veins in the undulating Nipissing diabase sill. This mining activity has resulted in the sill being well mapped geologically and dated radiometrically. Elsewhere the Nipissing diabase gives good paleomagnetic results. This paleomag- netic study was made to test whether the Miller Lake basinal structure defined by the sill at Gowganda is a primary intrusive or a secondary deformational feature by using the fold test on the sill's remanence directions from sites around the basin (Fig. 2, sites 1-23). This study was also made to test for possible geotectonic movements within the enclosing Superior Geologic Province or between it and other Precambrian provinces by comparing the sill's paleomagnetic pole position to other coeval poles from North America. Can. J. Earth Sci., 12,940-948 (1975) Geology The Gowganda area has been mapped geolog- ically by Collins (1913), Burrows (1921, 1926) and Moore (1955). Nipissing diabase were collected from around the Miller Lake basin at Gowganda. After alternatingfield demagnetization a stable primary remanence was isolated at 10 sites of which eight were reversely polarized. A fold test shows that the basinal structure is primary at the 95% confidence level. The pole position of 1M0W, 14"s (P0,,,:9", 14") is statistically indistinguishable from previous Nipissing poles from the Cobalt and Elliot Lake areas. The evident conclusion is that the Superior and Southern geologic provinces have not undergone significant relative tectonic translation or rotation in the last 2165 m.y. Combining the remanence directions from the 37 available reliable sites of Nipissing diabase, they give a highly reliable pole position of 94. low, 14.5"s (Po.,,:5.7", 8.8") for Nipissing time on the polar wander curve for these two provinces of the Canadian Precambrian Shield. Only four of the 37 sites are normally polarized suggesting that the Nipissing event reflects a dominantly reversed paleofield. The disper- sion of directions is a measure of the individual departures from the applied field owing to anisotropy. Methods Samples were collected from a total of 23 sites, 13 of which were situated in sediments and 10 in igneous rocks. At each of the sedi- mentary sites 3 or 4 hand samples were col- lected, yielding a total of 40 blocks. The igneous samples were collected by both field- drilling (36 cores) and hand-sampling (1 3 blocks). Most samples were oriented using a sun-compass. Due to overcast conditions some sedimentary samples were oriented magnetically. Comparison of magnetic and solar bearings, where possible, indicates that orientation errors do not exceed 5 " . All measurements of remanence were made on a commercial spinner magnetometer and routine partial demagnetization studies have been carried out on all specimens used in the final analysis. Alternating field (a.f. ) demag- netization was performed with an apparatus closely similar to that described by McElhinny ( 1966). Thermal cleaning experiments em- ployed a small furnace located in a room-sized magnetic shield similar to that described by Patton and Fitch (1962); the magnetic field over the volume occupied by the specimens is not more than 5y. The procedure adopted involves step-wise partial demagnetization (by both methods) of one pilot specimen per sample and analysis of the results in terms of within-site scatter. Received March 26, 1973 Revision accepted for publication June 15, 1973 Oriented samples of the Martin Formation were collected from 23 sites, both sediments and igneous rocks being represented. Detailed laboratory treatment yields an overall mean direction corresponding to a paleomagnetic pole at 9" S, 72" W (dp = 6.3", dm = 11.5"). Strong evidence for the primary nature of the magnetization involved is provided by a positive fold test. The paleomagnetic pole obtained pro- vides further evidence for a major eastward loop in the polar wandering path for North America during late Aphebian - early Helikian times. The exact age of Martin Formation deposition is the subject of debate, but extreme limits given by various authors are 1930 to 1490 m.y. However, the paleomagnetic results themselves somewhat restrict this range, and are of use in setting up a regional chronology, since they enable stratigraphic correlations between isolated sedimentary basins of the Canadian Shield to be made. The specimens have been classified into three groups, based on their stability of natural remanent magnetism, using the alternating field demagnetization technique. At sites 30NE and 33 the inclinations are lower. The approximate, but inexact, agreement between dykes and their contact rocks is a common effect, and is presumably caused by interaction between the fields of contact and diabase as they become magnetized at somewhat different times (Irving et al., 1972; Park, in press). At greater distances from the Indin dykes, notably in Dogrib diabase around Yellowknife, the directions are very different. Hence the contact test shows that the magnetization of the Indin dykes was probably acquired at the time of cooling. Any pervasive later magnetization event would also have remagne- tized the Dogrib diabase in the same direction, which it has not. Other, less well-documented data from a third dyke swarm (the “X” dykes) and a basic sill (the Duck Lake Sill), are also presented, and a very tentative polar path for the Slave Province in the earlier Proterozoic is given. This path is not greatly different from a similar very tentative early Aphebian polar path from the Archean Superior Province, consider- ing the uncertainties in the paleomagnetic and age determinations. The approximate, but inexact, agreement between dykes and their contact rocks is a common effect, and is presumably caused by interaction between the fields of contact and diabase as they become magnetized at somewhat different times (Irving et al., 1972; Park, in press). Ac- curacy of measurements were estimated to be within 5 degrees. Alternating field (A.F.) and thermal demagnetization was performed on standard equipment described by Mc- Elhinny (1963) and Phillips (1964). THESIS The radiometric data imply a difference in age of no more than 70 m.y. between the alkali granite and the poststructure basic granophyre (Nicolaysen et al. 1963). If the alkali-granite masses were intruded after the overturning, their primary remanent magnetism should be similar to that of the basic granophyre, assuming restricted polar wander during this short interval. On the other hand, if the alkali granites were in- truded before overturning, they should have been rotated with the collar rocks, through angles ranging up to 130 degrees. If their primary remanence survives the overturn- ing, the hypothesis predicts a specific angu- lar relationship between the vectors of the alkali granite and the basic granophyre. Good data, however, were obtained from the third, outer alkali-granite mass, and from olivine gabbro of the Rietfontein Complex, with which it is closely associated. The magnetic vectors from these two rock masses are about 54 degrees apart, suggesting differential structural rotation. When compared with the vector of the poststructure basic granophyre, however, they are both displaced more than 90 degrees before, and less than 30 degrees after, correction for overturning. It is therefore concluded that the basic igneous complex and the outer alkali granite on the farm Rietfontein, and presumably the other two alkali-granite plutons as well, were intruded prior to the development of the Vredefort Ring structure. The ring must have formed in the 70 m.y. or less between the times of emplacement of the granites and the basic granophyre, and could have been produced by impact.
